newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Post-vote crisis paralyzes Nicaraguan economy.
newsitem.headline: Post-vote crisis paralyzes Nicaraguan economy.

text.p: Political uncertainty surrounding Nicaragua's unresolved Oct. 20 general elections has taken a drastic toll on the economy as business has reported a slowdown in all sectors.

More than two weeks after the vote, apparently won by Arnoldo Aleman of the right-wing Liberal Alliance, Nicaragua's Supreme Election Council (CSE) still has not announced official winners amid rising charges of irregularities and fraud by the second-place leftist Sandinista Front.

While the pro-business Aleman has already claimed victory, Sandinista candidate Daniel Ortega, trailing Aleman 49 percent to 38 percent in the preliminary count, has refused to concede defeat, saying he wants the election council to review the vote count first.

The Sandinistas' refusal to concede has caused political tensions to soar as party activists with a history of militant protest have threatened a wave of protests if they are "robbed of their victory" by alleged Liberal fraud.
Police have banned public demonstrations and President Violeta Chamorro has called for calm, urging the CSE to hurry up and announce the winners to avoid political unrest.
In his empty appliance showroom in Managua, Raul Montenegro said business had dwindled to almost nothing because of the post-election crisis.
"People want to be sure of the political future of this country before they make a major investment. In this country politics and economics have always been hand in hand," he said.
During Nicaragua's 1979-1990 Sandinista socialist government, headed by Ortega, the state confiscated private property and introduced a planned economy with Soviet and Cuban backing.

President Chamorro, elected in 1990, returned the country to the capitalist fold. However, Nicaragua's fledgling free-market institutions are still delicate, especially laws regulating private property.
In the days before the election, Nicaragua's business community supported Aleman despite Ortega's apparent conversion from revolutionary to moderate social democrat.
As people in Nicaragua and abroad nervously await the results, business has come to a crunching slowdown, a statement from the Nicaraguan Union of Small and Medium-Sized Businesses (Unipyme) said.

Unipyme said the "fear and uncertainty" created by delays in the announcement of the winners is "to blame for the economic recession the country's large, medium and small industries are currently experiencing."
"A survey of our members has confirmed that their activities have been completely paralysed," it said.

Unipyme said customers on credit had stopped paying their debts and foreign suppliers had withdrawn from Nicaragua as they await the official vote results and the subsequent reactions by the losing parties.
Tax collectors in the capital of Managua have said municipal revenues are sharply down as people are putting off paying their taxes until they see who will sit in the mayor's chair.
The official announcement of winners is expected in mid- November at the earliest.
Meanwhile, Aleman, the 50-year-old former mayor of Managua, has urged the CSE to confirm his victory so that he can begin rebuilding Nicaragua's economy.
"I think that for Nicaragua's sake we must begin the reconstruction process. We can't wait anymore," he told reporters.
